b: Heavyweight walleyes historically migrate to the eastern basin of Lake Ontario in fall. And New York anglers Craig Sleeman and Keith Hagenbuch had enjoyed some good runs there with several trips targeting big “eyes” on the sprawling Great Lake.
“We had one trip where we caught and released about 20 walleyes,” Sleeman told Wired2fish. “Most of them were five to seven pounds, but we’ve caught nine-pounders, too.”
The two were fishing on Halloween morning out of Sleeman’s Ranger walleye boat, using forward-facing sonar to pinpoint big walleyes for casting.

“There was no wind and the surface was glass smooth,” said the 46-year-old high school teacher from Phelps, New York. “It was a pretty tough bite early that morning. But about mid-morning, fish started to turn on if we made very long casts in that clear lake.”
They were fishing in 35 feet of water at about 10:30 a.m. Then, Sleeman spotted a large mark on his Garmin sonar.

“The fish was alone, and I’ve found that reaction bites this time of year are best because the water temp is in the mid-50s and the fish are slowing down,” he said. “I made a long cast with a Rip-N-Glide 5/8s ounce lure with a custom paint job of tan and white to look like a goby baitfish.

“When the lure got down to the level of the sonar mark nothing happened. I let the lure sit on bottom for a moment, then started sliding it across rocks making it look like a real goby minnow with small twitches.”
Sleeman had a strike and the fish was strong, fighting like a freshwater drum.
“It had some juice, too, taking some drag against my spinning reel,” he said. “I fought it for two or three minutes, and for a while I thought maybe I foul hooked a fish.”
But as he worked it to the surface he spotted it down about eight feet and knew it was a giant walleye.
Hagenbuch netted it and they quickly measured its length at 30 inches, weighing it on a digital Bubba scale at 13 pounds, two ounces. Then they took some photos and released it.
They fished for a while longer, then headed for home about 1 p.m. to join with family trick-or-treat holiday traditions.
Sleeman, who’s getting a replica mount of his giant 13-pounder, noted that there is still some great fishing for huge walleyes in the lake’s eastern reaches.

“That part of the lake is known by anglers as the Golden Crescent, and it has great walleye fishing through the fall and then into the winter through the ice,” he explained. “Some of the great bays to fish walleyes there include Henderson, Chaumont, and around Galloo Island and Calf Island.
“It’s also a good area for big smallmouths.”
